 State Police all over New England just handed out 6,000 traffic citations, 2,000 speeding tickets, and made 36 drunken driving busts. (MSP photo) 
 By Joe Dwinell | joed@bostonherald.com | Boston Herald PUBLISHED: October 19, 2026 at 6:36 PM EDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... The State Police all over New England targeted reckless road warriors, handing out 6,000 traffic citations in “Operation Wicked Safe.”
 The agencies also combined to make 36 OUI arrests and issue more than 2,000 speeding tickets in the October 13-15 operation.
 “Operation Wicked Safe sent a clear message that dangerous and distracted driving will not be tolerated on our roadways,” said Massachusetts State Police Colonel Geoffrey Noble. “By coordinating our efforts with five neighboring agencies, we expanded our enforcement presence across state lines and reinforced our shared commitment to protecting everyone who travels our roads.”
 State Police agencies from Massachusetts, Connecticut, New Hampshire, New York, Rhode Island and Vermont joined forces in the sweep.
 Noble said the officers will be back on patrol.
 Blood-alcohol limit
 Two alleged drunken drivers blowing a 0.157% and 0.128% blood-alcohol roadside test, respectively, were at risk of blacking out.
 Southboro police said the suspects were both charged with drunken driving. Wilber P. Chinchilla, 30, of Framingham, was arrested on Route 9 at about 2 a.m. during a “routine traffic stop” where police said they discovered “several nips and an open tequila bottle.” He blew a 0.157% BAC.
 Isabella Tofani, 25, of Marlboro, was pulled over also on Monday at 2:50 a.m. after police said they spotted “a green Subaru SUV driving erratically in close proximity to the vehicle in front of it.”
 “While speaking to the operator of the vehicle … officers detected a strong odor of alcohol on her person. Following an investigation, including field sobriety tests, and a breathalyzer test which registered a blood alcohol content of 0.128%, Tofani was arrested without incident,” police added.
 Both were arraigned in Westboro District Court the same day.
 Pre-Halloween warning
 The “Buzzed Driving is Drunk Driving” campaign is gearing up for the Halloween party season.
 From 2020 to 2024, 201 people were killed in alcohol-related crashes, which involve at least one driver who had a blood alcohol level of .01 or higher, on the night of Halloween, according to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration.
 Drivers should secure a designated sober driver or call a taxi or rideshare for a sober ride home, because “Buzzed Driving Is Drunk Driving.” For more information on impaired driving, visit NHTSA.gov/DrunkDriving .
 Mother arraigned
 Jillian Timmons. (Abington Police Department) 
 An Abington woman was arraigned Monday in Brockton Superior Court on charges of abusing her 2-month-old child “that caused severe injuries,” Plymouth District Attorney Timothy J. Cruz announced.
 Jillian Timmons, 34, is charged with on one count each of assault and battery on a child causing serious bodily injury and reckless endangerment of a child.
 She was placed on $20,000 cash bail and ordered to stay away and have no contact with her child unless supervised by the state Department of Children and Families or at the request of a healthcare professional.
 Timmons was also ordered to stay away and have no contact with an alleged co-defendant.
 The DA added: “A mandated reporter at South Shore Hospital contacted authorities about the suspected physical abuse of Timmons’ daughter, after Timmons brought her into the hospital for treatment.”
 BPD Most Wanted
 Boston Police are seeking the public’s help in catching the most wanted in the city.
 BPD says if you know anything about the whereabouts of any of these individuals call CrimeStoppers Tip Line at 1 (800) 494-TIPS (8477) or text the word ‘TIP’ to CRIME (27463). The Boston Police Department is interested only in your information, not your identity. Your tip is 100% anonymous.
 Calls or texts to CrimeStoppers are answered by Police Officers and trained personnel who forward the information to the appropriate investigators. “You do not have to reveal your identity to the police to provide information about a crime,” BPD adds.
